claim: FXR is activated by its physiological ligands, bile acids (BAs).
source: FXR is activated by its physiological ligands, bile acids (BAs), and regulates expression of genes involved in BA, lipid, and glucose metabolism and hepatic autophagy, which maintain metabolite levels and metabolic homeostasis (Calkin and Tontonoz, 2012; Kliewer and Mangelsdorf, 2015; Lee et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2014; Seok et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research establishing FXR activation by bile acids.

claim: FXR regulates expression of genes involved in BA, lipid, and glucose metabolism and hepatic autophagy.
source: FXR is activated by its physiological ligands, bile acids (BAs), and regulates expression of genes involved in BA, lipid, and glucose metabolism and hepatic autophagy, which maintain metabolite levels and metabolic homeostasis (Calkin and Tontonoz, 2012; Kliewer and Mangelsdorf, 2015; Lee et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2014; Seok et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on FXR's regulatory functions.

claim: Ligand-activated FXR protects against hepatic inflammation and liver injury.
source: Ligand-activated FXR also protects against hepatic inflammation and liver injury (Jung et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research demonstrating FXR's protective effects.

claim: FXR is increasingly recognized as a promising drug target for liver diseases, such as NASH and primary biliary cholangitis (PBC).
source: Consistent with its crucial physiological functions, FXR is increasingly recognized as a promising drug target, particularly for liver diseases, such as NASH and primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) (Abenavoli et al., 2018; Ali et al., 2015; Downes et al., 2003; Kremoser, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and reviews on FXR as a therapeutic target.

claim: Tropifexor and cilofexor are currently in clinical trials for NASH and PBC patients.
source: For example, semi-synthetic or non-steroidal synthetic agonists of FXR, including obeticholic acid (OCA) and hammerhead-type agonists, such as tropifexor and cilofexor, are currently in clinical trials for NASH and PBC patients (Abenavoli et al., 2018; Kremoser, 2021; Sanyal et al., 2023; Tully et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical trial literature.

claim: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are a group of transcripts longer than 200 nucleotides.
source: Of these ncRNAs, long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are a group of transcripts longer than 200 nucleotides and play important roles in diverse biological processes (Lam et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016; Mattick et al., 2023; Sartorelli and Lauberth, 2020; Statello et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research defining lncRNAs and their roles.

claim: Enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) are transcribed from transcriptional enhancers, with >85k in humans and >57k in mice.
source: This is consistent with the idea that many transcriptional enhancers actively transcribe ncRNAs that are referred to as enhancer RNAs (eRNAs, >85k in humans and >57k in mice) (Hirabayashi et al., 2019), some of which are functionally important for enhancer functions (Lai and Shiekhattar, 2014; Li et al., 2016; Sartorelli and Lauberth, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on eRNA prevalence and function.

claim: FXR was shown to regulate expression of small non-coding microRNA (miR) genes, e.g., Mir34a and Mir802.
source: FXR was shown to regulate expression of small non-coding microRNA (miR) genes, e.g., Mir34a and Mir802 (Lee et al., 2010; Seok et al., 2021), but it has not been reported whether FXR achieves its function through regulating lncRNAs, which far outnumber miRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on FXR regulation of microRNAs.

claim: 190 high-confidence eRNAs were identified in mouse liver.
source: This genomic analysis resulted in identification of 190 high-confidence eRNAs in mouse liver.
evidence: This claim is based on the RNA-seq and genomic analysis performed in this study.

claim: 14 eRNAs were upregulated and 5 were downregulated by GW4064 treatment (FDR <0.05, log2FC >1).
source: Among these, 14 eRNAs were upregulated and 5 were downregulated by GW4064 treatment (FDR <0.05, log2FC >1, Figure 1A) (see Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary files.

claim: Fincor is one of the most robustly induced eRNAs by GW4064 treatment.
source: One of the most robustly induced eRNAs was Fincor, an unannotated novel transcript located on chromosome 19 (Figure 1A, B, and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A, B, and C.

claim: GW4064 treatment substantially induced expression of Fincor, more than 10-fold in mouse liver.
source: Reverse transcription qPCR (RT-qPCR) confirmed that treatment with GW4064 substantially induced expression of Fincor, more than 10-fold in mouse liver, which is similar to induction of Nr0b2, a well-known FXR target gene (Figure 1D; Claudel et al., 2005; Evans and Mangelsdorf, 2014; Goodwin et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Induction of Fincor by GW4064 was transient, peaked within 1 hr and then declined gradually.
source: Induction of Fincor by GW4064 was transient, peaked within 1 hr and then declined gradually, a pattern similar to that of Nr0b2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by time course data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Expression of genes adjacent to Fincor, including Gcnt1, Rfk, Pcsk5, and Prune2, did not change after acute 1 hr FXR activation.
source: Expression of genes adjacent to Fincor, including Gcnt1, Rfk, Pcsk5, and Prune2, did not change after acute 1 hr FXR activation as shown by RNA-seq (Figure 1C), and confirmed for Gcnt1 by time course qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 1C and qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Short-time GW4064 treatment resulted in 590 upregulated genes and 500 downregulated genes (FDR <0.05).
source: We also found that the short-time GW4064 treatment resulted in 590 upregulated genes and 500 downregulated genes (FDR <0.05) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: FXR-induced eRNAs were activated transcriptionally by GW4064 in Fxr-flox mice, but such induction was abolished in Fxr-LKO mice.
source: GRO-seq showed that FXR-induced eRNAs were activated transcriptionally by GW4064 in Fxr-flox mice, but such induction was abolished in Fxr-LKO mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Fincor is robustly induced in the GRO-seq analysis and its induction is dependent on hepatic FXR.
source: In particular, Fincor is robustly induced in the GRO-seq analysis and its induction is dependent on hepatic FXR (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GRO-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FXR binding was strongly enriched at the enhancers associated with FXR-induced eRNAs.
source: FXR binding was strongly enriched at the enhancers associated with FXR-induced eRNAs as were the enhancer marks H3K27ac and H3K4me1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GW4064 treatment resulted in substantial increases in recruitment of both FXR and RXRα to the enhancer region close to the transcription start site of Fincor.
source: GW4064 treatment resulted in substantial increases in recruitment of both FXR and RXRα to the enhancer region close to the transcription start site of Fincor (arrow shown below in Figure 2B), whereas binding was not detected at a control region (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: BRD4 occupancy was increased at the Fincor enhancer region after GW4064 treatment.
source: We also found that BRD4 occupancy was increased at this enhancer region after GW4064 treatment (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: An inverted repeat1 (IR1) motif that is known to bind FXR was identified within the major FXR binding peak near the start site of Fincor.
source: We identified an inverted repeat1 (IR1) motif that is known to bind FXR (Calkin and Tontonoz, 2012; Lee et al., 2006) within the major FXR binding peak near the start site of Fincor (arrow shown below in Figure 2B), which we also refer to as FXRE (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B and C, along with citations to prior research on FXR binding motifs.

claim: GW4064 treatment significantly elevated the luciferase activity of the reporter with the wild-type IR1 motif, but not with the mutated IR1 motif.
source: After transfection into human hepatic HepG2 cells, GW4064 treatment significantly elevated the luciferase activity of the reporter with the wild-type IR1 motif, but not with the mutated IR1 motif (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Fincor is highly expressed in the liver and it is expressed at extremely low levels in most other tissues, except for a detectable, but still fairly low, level in the lung.
source: Strikingly, Fincor is highly expressed in the liver and it is expressed at extremely low levels in most other tissues, except for a detectable, but still fairly low, level in the lung (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GW4064 treatment resulted in induction of Fincor specifically in the liver.
source: GW4064 treatment resulted in induction of Fincor specifically in the liver (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The level of Fincor detected in primary mouse hepatocytes (PMHs) isolated from GW4064-treated mouse liver was similar to that in the liver tissue from the same mouse.
source: The level of Fincor detected in primary mouse hepatocytes (PMHs) isolated from GW4064-treated mouse liver was similar to that in the liver tissue from the same mouse, suggesting that the majority of Fincor is present in hepatocytes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data comparing liver tissue and primary hepatocytes shown in Figure 3B.

claim: One transcript of Fincor is approximately 3.7 kb in length.
source: By using the 5' and 3' rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE), we identified one transcript of Fincor that is approximately 3.7 kb in length (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RACE data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Based on RNA-seq, the length of Fincor is over 10 kb, suggesting there are likely additional multiple RNA isoforms.
source: However, based on RNA-seq, the length of Fincor is over 10 kb (Figure 1C), suggesting there are likely additional multiple RNA isoforms that we were not able to identify by RACE.
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and inference from the discrepancy with RACE results.

claim: Fincor did not contain a potential protein-coding open reading frame according to PhyloCSF analysis.
source: We next analyzed the coding potential of Fincor utilizing a comparative genomic program, PhyloCSF. While adjacent genes Gcnt1 and Prune2 (Figure 3D and E) were correctly predicted to encode proteins, Fincor did not contain a potential protein-coding open reading frame (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by PhyloCSF analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A vector expressing Fincor failed to produce any proteins in an in vitro transcription/translation assay.
source: Consistent with this bioinformatic prediction, a vector expressing Fincor failed to produce any proteins in an in vitro transcription/translation assay (Figure 3F), confirming that the Fincor transcript is an ncRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro translation assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Fincor transcripts were enriched by binding to oligo-dT beads, suggesting that Fincor is 3' polyadenylated.
source: Fincor transcripts were enriched by binding to oligo-dT beads, suggesting that Fincor is 3' polyadenylated (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by poly(A) enrichment data shown in Figure 3G and inference about polyadenylation.

claim: Fincor was detected in the nuclear compartment and GW4064 treatment increased the nuclear abundance of Fincor.
source: Further, Fincor was detected in the nuclear compartment and GW4064 treatment increased the nuclear abundance of Fincor (Figure 3H), consistent with its potential transcriptional regulatory function.
evidence: This claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Treatment with each of the hammerhead-type agonists (GW4064, cilofexor, and tropifexor) for 1 hr resulted in a robust induction of Fincor.
source: Remarkably, treatment with each of the hammerhead-type agonists for 1 hr resulted in a robust induction of Fincor (Figure 4B), whereas Fincor levels were unchanged after treatment with OCA or fexaramine for 1 hr (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Fincor levels were unchanged after treatment with OCA or fexaramine for 1 hr.
source: Remarkably, treatment with each of the hammerhead-type agonists for 1 hr resulted in a robust induction of Fincor (Figure 4B), whereas Fincor levels were unchanged after treatment with OCA or fexaramine for 1 hr (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Treatment with OCA for 4 hr or even 1 week treatment with OCA failed to induce hepatic Fincor in mice.
source: Treatment with OCA for 4 hr or even 1 week treatment with OCA failed to induce hepatic Fincor in mice, while expression of Nr0b2 was significantly induced (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Acute feeding with a diet supplemented with 0.5% cholic acid (CA) for 6 hr failed to induce Fincor expression.
source: Acute feeding with a diet supplemented with 0.5% cholic acid (CA), a primary BA, for 6 hr also failed to induce Fincor expression (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Adenoviral-mediated sgRNA expression in Cas9 mice resulted in downregulation of Fincor specifically in the liver by about 60%, but not in other tissues.
source: Adenoviral-mediated sgRNA expression in Cas9 mice resulted in downregulation of Fincor specifically in the liver by about 60%, but not in other tissues (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fincor downregulation did not result in any significant changes in liver triglyceride, cholesterol, BA, glycogen, and serum non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA) under physiological conditions.
source: We examined liver triglyceride, cholesterol, BA, glycogen, and serum non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA) but Fincor downregulation did not result in any significant changes under physiological conditions (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolic measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: RNA-seq analysis revealed 18 upregulated genes and 53 downregulated genes in Fincor-LKD liver.
source: The RNA-seq analysis revealed 18 upregulated genes and 53 downregulated genes in Fincor-LKD liver (Supplementary file 2; Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E and Supplementary file 2.

claim: While Fincor was markedly downregulated, the neighboring genes, such as Gcnt1, Rfk, Pcsk5, and Prune2, were largely unchanged.
source: While Fincor was markedly downregulated, the neighboring genes, such as Gcnt1, Rfk, Pcsk5, and Prune2, were largely unchanged (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Downregulated genes in Fincor-LKD liver were enriched in pathways involved in fatty acid oxidation, organelle organization, and metabolic process.
source: GO analysis of those downregulated genes indicated that these genes were enriched in pathways involved in fatty acid oxidation, organelle organization, and metabolic process (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Fincor levels were significantly increased by FXR agonist tropifexor, and the increase was blocked by adenovirus expressing sgRNA for Fincor.
source: In these mice, as a technical validation of RNA induction and knockdown, Fincor levels were significantly increased by FXR agonist tropifexor, and the increase was blocked by adenovirus expressing sgRNA for Fincor (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tropifexor treatment markedly reduced neutral lipids determined by Oil Red O staining of liver sections and liver TG levels.
source: Tropifexor treatment markedly reduced neutral lipids determined by Oil Red O staining of liver sections (Figure 6C) and liver TG levels (Figure 6D), and these beneficial effects on reducing fatty liver were not altered by Fincor downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil Red O staining and TG measurement data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The beneficial effects of tropifexor on reducing fatty liver were not altered by Fincor downregulation.
source: Tropifexor treatment markedly reduced neutral lipids determined by Oil Red O staining of liver sections (Figure 6C) and liver TG levels (Figure 6D), and these beneficial effects on reducing fatty liver were not altered by Fincor downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil Red O staining and TG measurement data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Tropifexor treatment reduced hepatic expression of key genes involved in BA synthesis (Cyp7a1 and Cyp8b1).
source: Consistent with the phenotypes, hepatic expression of key genes involved in BA synthesis was dramatically reduced by tropifexor treatment (i.e. Cyp7a1 and Cyp8b1), which is consistent with decreased gallbladder BA levels mediated by this agonist (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Tropifexor lowered lipid synthesis genes (Srebp1c, Lpin1, Scd1), consistent with decreased liver TG levels.
source: Similarly, tropifexor also lowered lipid synthesis genes (Srebp1c, Lpin1, Scd1), consistent with decreased liver TG levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data and is consistent with TG measurements.

claim: Downregulation of Fincor did not result in changes in mRNA levels of genes involved in BA and lipid synthesis.
source: However, downregulation of Fincor did not result in changes in mRNA levels of these genes (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Tropifexor treatment reduced hepatocyte swelling/ballooning, decreased numbers of apoptotic cells, alleviated fibrosis, and lowered infiltration of macrophages.
source: In the same AMLN diet-fed mice as described above (Figure 6), analyses of liver sections revealed that tropifexor treatment reduced hepatocyte swelling/ballooning (hematoxylin and eosin [H&E] staining), decreased numbers of apoptotic cells (TUNEL staining), alleviated fibrosis (Sirius Red staining), and lowered infiltration of macrophages (F4/80 staining) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological staining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Tropifexor-mediated beneficial effects on NASH pathologies were all markedly diminished by Fincor downregulation.
source: Remarkably, these tropifexor-mediated beneficial effects on NASH pathologies were all markedly diminished by Fincor downregulation (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological staining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Serum ALT and AST levels were significantly elevated after Fincor downregulation.
source: Consistent with these results, serum ALT and AST levels, indicators of liver damage, were significantly elevated after Fincor downregulation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by serum enzyme measurement data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Protein levels of key inflammatory markers, IL1β and CCL2, in liver extracts were elevated after Fincor downregulation.
source: Protein levels of key inflammatory markers, IL1β and CCL2, in liver extracts were also elevated after Fincor downregulation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Tropifexor treatment reduced mRNA levels of several genes that promote fibrosis (Col1a1, Col1a2, Acta2) and hepatic inflammation (Eda2r, Ifng, Ccl3), whereas these reductions were largely reversed by Fincor downregulation.
source: For example, tropifexor treatment reduced mRNA levels of several genes that promote fibrosis (Col1a1, Col1a2, Acta2) and hepatic inflammation (Eda2r, Ifng, Ccl3), whereas these reductions were largely reversed by Fincor downregulation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Increased expression of inflammatory genes (Ccl2, Ccr2, Lcn2) and an extracellular matrix remodeling gene (Fndc1) was detected in liver with Fincor knockdown.
source: We also detected increased expression of inflammatory genes (Ccl2, Ccr2, Lcn2) and an extracellular matrix remodeling gene (Fndc1) in liver with Fincor knockdown (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Tropifexor treatment suppressed hepatic apoptosis by reducing pro-apoptotic genes (Ctsb, Ctss) and upregulating anti-apoptotic genes such as Bcl2, and these effects were significantly reversed by Fincor downregulation.
source: Tropifexor treatment suppressed hepatic apoptosis by reducing pro-apoptotic genes (Ctsb, Ctss) and upregulating anti-apoptotic genes such as Bcl2 (Warren et al., 2019). Importantly, these effects were significantly reversed by Fincor downregulation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7D and a citation to prior research on Bcl2.

claim: Hepatic Fincor levels were significantly increased in mice fed with a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks.
source: Hepatic Fincor levels were significantly increased in mice fed with a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks (Figure 8A) and in mice fed an HFD with high fructose in drinking water for 12 weeks (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Hepatic Fincor levels were significantly increased in mice fed an HFD with high fructose in drinking water for 12 weeks.
source: Hepatic Fincor levels were significantly increased in mice fed with a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks (Figure 8A) and in mice fed an HFD with high fructose in drinking water for 12 weeks (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Elevated hepatic Fincor levels were observed in mice treated with α-naphthylisothiocyanate (ANIT), a chemical inducer of liver cholestasis.
source: Elevated hepatic Fincor levels were also observed in mice treated with α-naphthylisothiocyanate (ANIT), a chemical inducer of liver cholestasis (Jung et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2016; Figure 8C), and in mice with bile duct ligation (BDL), a surgical method to induce cholestatic liver injury (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8C and citations to prior research on ANIT.

claim: Elevated hepatic Fincor levels were observed in mice with bile duct ligation (BDL), a surgical method to induce cholestatic liver injury.
source: Elevated hepatic Fincor levels were also observed in mice treated with α-naphthylisothiocyanate (ANIT), a chemical inducer of liver cholestasis (Jung et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2016; Figure 8C), and in mice with bile duct ligation (BDL), a surgical method to induce cholestatic liver injury (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The sequence of Fincor is moderately conserved between mice and humans.
source: The sequence of Fincor is moderately conserved between mice and humans as displayed in the UCSC genome browser (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Annotation in the NCBI genome data viewer of the human sequence region with similarity to mouse Fincor revealed an functionally uncharacterized human lncRNA, XR_007061585.1.
source: Annotation in the NCBI genome data viewer of the human sequence region with similarity to mouse Fincor revealed an functionally uncharacterized human lncRNA, XR_007061585.1, in this region (Figure 8F).
evidence: This claim is supported by genome annotation data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Hepatic lncRNA XR_007061585.1 levels were elevated in patients with PBC or NAFLD compared to normal individuals.
source: Compared to normal individuals, hepatic lncRNA XR_007061585.1 levels were elevated in patients with PBC or NAFLD, but not in severe NASH-fibrosis patients (Figure 8G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from human liver samples shown in Figure 8G and H.

claim: Hepatic lncRNA XR_007061585.1 levels were not elevated in severe NASH-fibrosis patients.
source: Compared to normal individuals, hepatic lncRNA XR_007061585.1 levels were elevated in patients with PBC or NAFLD, but not in severe NASH-fibrosis patients (Figure 8G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from human liver samples shown in Figure 8G and H.

claim: Pharmacological activation of FXR by hammerhead-type agonists induces a novel eRNA, Fincor, contributing to the amelioration of NASH in mice.
source: Overall, our findings highlight that pharmacological activation of FXR by hammerhead-type agonists induces a novel eRNA, Fincor, contributing to the amelioration of NASH in mice.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Fincor may represent a new drug target for addressing metabolic disorders, including NASH.
source: Fincor may represent a new drug target for addressing metabolic disorders, including NASH.
evidence: This claim is a speculative conclusion based on the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: NAFLD is the most common chronic liver disease and a leading cause of liver transplants and liver-related death.
source: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common chronic liver disease and a leading cause of liver transplants and liver-related death (Friedman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on NAFLD epidemiology.

claim: NAFLD begins with simple steatosis but may further progress to a severe form, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and later, fatal cirrhosis and liver cancer.
source: NAFLD begins with simple steatosis but may further progress to a severe form, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and later, fatal cirrhosis and liver cancer (Friedman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on NAFLD disease progression.

claim: There is no approved drug for NASH.
source: Despite its striking global increase and clinical importance, there is no approved drug for NASH.
evidence: This claim reflects the current state of NASH therapeutics at the time of manuscript writing.

claim: FXR directly regulates expression of its target genes.
source: Because FXR directly regulates expression of its target genes (Lee et al., 2012; Thomas et al., 2010), we examined if FXR regulates eRNAs, and if such transcripts participate in its physiological or pharmacological functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on FXR's direct regulatory functions.

claim: Tropifexor is a highly potent hammerhead-type FXR agonist that is currently under clinical trials for NASH and PBC patients.
source: Tropifexor, also known as LJN452, is a highly potent hammerhead-type FXR agonist that is currently under clinical trials for NASH and PBC patients (Kremoser, 2021; Sanyal et al., 2023; Tully et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical trial literature.

claim: In diet-induced NASH mice, pharmacological activation of FXR by tropifexor reduced fibrosis, apoptosis, and inflammation, which was dependent, at least in part, on the induction of Fincor.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that in diet-induced NASH mice, pharmacological activation of FXR by tropifexor reduced fibrosis, apoptosis, and inflammation, which was dependent, at least in part, on the induction of Fincor.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Tropifexor-mediated beneficial effects on reducing hepatic steatosis are independent of Fincor.
source: These results indicate that tropifexor-mediated beneficial effects on reducing hepatic steatosis are independent of Fincor.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Fincor is required for tropifexor-mediated beneficial effects on reducing NASH pathologies, specifically reducing hepatic inflammation, fibrosis, and hepatocyte apoptosis.
source: These results demonstrate that Fincor is required for tropifexor-mediated beneficial effects on reducing NASH pathologies, specifically reducing hepatic inflammation, fibrosis, and hepatocyte apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Amelioration of liver fibrosis and inflammation in NASH treatment by tropifexor is mediated in part by Fincor.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated liver-specific knockdown of Fincor in dietary NASH mice reduced the beneficial effects of tropifexor, an FXR agonist currently in clinical trials for NASH and primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), indicating that amelioration of liver fibrosis and inflammation in NASH treatment by tropifexor is mediated in part by Fincor.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fincor is a liver-enriched enhancer-derived lncRNA (eRNA).
source: Among these we discovered a previously unannotated liver-enriched enhancer-derived lncRNA (eRNA), termed FXR-induced non-coding RNA (Fincor).
evidence: This claim is based on the characterization of Fincor presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fincor is specifically induced by the hammerhead-type FXR agonists, including GW4064 and tropifexor.
source: We show that Fincor is specifically induced by the hammerhead-type FXR agonists, including GW4064 and tropifexor.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: GW4064-activated FXR directly upregulates Fincor expression.
source: Together, these results suggest that GW4064-activated FXR directly upregulates Fincor expression.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Fincor is a liver-enriched nuclear polyadenylated eRNA.
source: Together, these results from molecular biochemical characterization studies reveal that Fincor is a liver-enriched nuclear polyadenylated eRNA.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on the characterization data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Fincor is induced specifically by hammerhead-type FXR agonists.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that Fincor is induced specifically by hammerhead-type FXR agonists.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Fincor has a role in modulating metabolic homeostasis by regulating genes involved in metabolism and inflammation.
source: These studies suggest that Fincor has a role in modulating metabolic homeostasis by regulating genes involved in metabolism and inflammation.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on the RNA-seq data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Hepatic levels of a potential human analog of Fincor are elevated in NAFLD and PBC patients.
source: These results demonstrate that hepatic levels of a potential human analog of Fincor are elevated in NAFLD and PBC patients, as Fincor is in mouse models of chronic liver disease with hepatic inflammation and liver injury.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on the human liver sample data presented in Figure 8G and H.

claim: FXR mediates its functions by induction of lncRNA genes.
source: In this study we show that FXR also mediates its functions by induction of lncRNA genes, which vastly outnumber protein-coding genes.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The gene signature regulated by tropifexor-activated FXR appears to be broader than that of OCA.
source: Intriguingly, a recent study showed that the gene signature regulated by tropifexor-activated FXR appears to be broader than that of OCA, partly because the tropifexor backbone allows a more favorable interaction of FXR with coactivators or epigenomic modulators (Hernandez et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research comparing tropifexor and OCA.

claim: Tropifexor was shown to regulate distinct sets of genes in experimental NASH as compared to other FXR agonists, particularly genes involved in fibrosis, inflammation, and oxidative stress.
source: Further, tropifexor was shown to regulate distinct sets of genes in experimental NASH as compared to other FXR agonists, particularly genes involved in fibrosis, inflammation, and oxidative stress (Hernandez et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on tropifexor's gene regulation.

claim: Beneficial effects on reducing liver fibrosis, inflammation, and apoptosis mediated by tropifexor were largely dependent on Fincor.
source: Utilizing CRISPR/Cas9-mediated liver-specific knockdown of Fincor in diet-induced NASH mice, we demonstrate that beneficial effects on reducing liver fibrosis, inflammation, and apoptosis mediated by tropifexor were largely dependent on Fincor (Model, Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Fincor may not contribute to the physiological functions of FXR.
source: Although Fincor can be induced by the hammerhead class of FXR agonists, it was not induced by the endogenous FXR ligand, CA. This implies that Fincor may not contribute to the physiological functions of FXR.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that CA does not induce Fincor.

claim: Fincor levels were elevated in mouse models of cholestasis and NASH.
source: In an effort to investigate the potential role of Fincor in the pathological conditions, we observed that Fincor levels were elevated in mouse models of cholestasis and NASH as well as in human PBC and NAFLD patients, where BA metabolism is dysregulated.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Binding peaks for multiple nuclear receptors, FXR, LXR, PPARα, RXRα, and HNF-4α, were detected in the Fincor locus.
source: Further, binding peaks for multiple nuclear receptors, FXR, LXR, PPARα, RXRα, and HNF-4α, were detected in the Fincor locus so that regulation of Fincor likely involves the combinatorial regulation by multiple nuclear receptors (Supplementary file 3a).
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 3a.

claim: Occupancy of the nuclear receptor PPARα at the enhancer region was increased in fasted mice.
source: Interestingly, occupancy of the nuclear receptor PPARα at the enhancer region was increased in fasted mice (Supplementary file 3b).
evidence: This claim is based on ChIP-seq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 3b.

claim: The roles of regulatory RNAs in liver function and diseases and their potentials as therapeutic targets are increasingly being appreciated.
source: The roles of regulatory RNAs in liver function and diseases and their potentials as therapeutic targets are increasingly being appreciated (Brocker et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Sallam et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on regulatory RNAs in liver biology.

claim: A critical role for an oxysterol nuclear receptor LXR-induced lncRNA, LeXis, in feedback modulation of cholesterol biosynthesis has been shown.
source: For example, a critical role for an oxysterol nuclear receptor LXR-induced lncRNA, LeXis, in feedback modulation of cholesterol biosynthesis has been shown (Sallam et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on the lncRNA LeXis.

claim: The role of an lncRNA, Pair, in liver phenylalanine metabolism has been demonstrated.
source: Recently, the role of an lncRNA, Pair, in liver phenylalanine metabolism has been demonstrated (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on the lncRNA Pair.

claim: Enhancer RNAs are a less-characterized class of lncRNAs and are highly associated with enhancer functions in gene regulation.
source: Enhancer RNAs are a less-characterized class of lncRNAs and are highly associated with enhancer functions in gene regulation (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on eRNAs.

claim: Most previous eRNA studies have used cultured cells, with only a few in vivo studies in mouse models.
source: Numerous studies have revealed transcriptional roles for eRNAs in various cellular processes (Lai and Shiekhattar, 2014; Lam et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016; Sartorelli and Lauberth, 2020) but most previous eRNA studies have used cultured cells (Hsieh et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013), with only a few in vivo studies in mouse models (Mirtschink et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on eRNA studies.

claim: The current work characterized the role of Fincor in gene regulation and in mediating beneficial pharmacological effects of tropifexor in NASH.
source: In our current study, through integrative analysis of transcriptome and histone mark ChIP-seq, we identified a group of FXR-regulated eRNAs, including the highly induced Fincor. Our current work characterized the role of Fincor in gene regulation and in mediating beneficial pharmacological effects of tropifexor in NASH, representing important progress in understanding the roles of eRNAs in vivo.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The top four candidates for Fincor binding are KHDRBS1, RBM38, YBX2, and YBX3.
source: We identified potential binding proteins of Fincor using the ATtRACT database (Giudice et al., 2016). The top four candidates for Fincor binding are KHDRBS1, RBM38, YBX2, and YBX3 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is based on bioinformatic analysis using the ATtRACT database.

claim: KHDRBS1 and RBM38 have been reported to have important roles in RNA processing.
source: KHDRBS1 and RBM38 have been reported to have important roles in RNA processing (Bielli et al., 2011; Zou et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on these RNA binding proteins.

claim: YBX2 and YBX3 belong to the Y-box (YBX) protein family, which have been linked to diverse forms of RNA metabolism and many other processes, including cell proliferation, DNA repair, stress responses, development, and inflammation.
source: YBX2 and YBX3 belong to the Y-box (YBX) protein family, which have been linked to diverse forms of RNA metabolism and many other processes, including cell proliferation, DNA repair, stress responses, development, and inflammation (Kleene, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on YBX proteins.

claim: The function of eRNA loci can be attributed to a functional eRNA transcript, or binding of transcription factors to this region, or the transcription process itself, or some combination of these effects.
source: Currently, the function of eRNA loci can be attributed to a functional eRNA transcript, or binding of transcription factors to this region, or the transcription process itself, or some combination of these effects (Li et al., 2016; Sartorelli and Lauberth, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on eRNA mechanisms.

claim: In the studies to decrease expression of Fincor, the region containing the FXR binding site was deleted.
source: In our studies to decrease expression of Fincor, the region containing the FXR binding site was deleted (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, right panel).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: FXR is increasingly recognized as an important therapeutic target for enterohepatic diseases.
source: FXR is increasingly recognized as an important therapeutic target for enterohepatic diseases, but the development of clinically applicable and more targeted FXR-based therapy is still challenging.
evidence: This claim reflects current knowledge about FXR as a therapeutic target.

claim: The development of clinically applicable and more targeted FXR-based therapy is still challenging.
source: FXR is increasingly recognized as an important therapeutic target for enterohepatic diseases, but the development of clinically applicable and more targeted FXR-based therapy is still challenging.
evidence: This claim reflects current challenges in FXR-based drug development.

claim: Fincor has a beneficial role in reducing liver fibrosis and inflammation in dietary NASH mice.
source: In this study, we provide the first characterization of an eRNA, Fincor, induced by pharmacological activation of FXR and show that Fincor has a beneficial role in reducing liver fibrosis and inflammation in dietary NASH mice.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Complete understanding of the function and mechanisms of Fincor may provide novel insights for the development of desirable therapy for NASH and other chronic liver diseases.
source: Complete understanding of the function and mechanisms of Fincor may provide novel insights for the development of desirable therapy for NASH and other chronic liver diseases.
evidence: This claim is a speculative conclusion about the potential therapeutic implications of the findings.
